abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Aberrant expression of microRNAs (miRNAs) is closely associated with the pathogenesis and progression of various diseases, particularly cancer, as well as therapeutic responses. Identification of miRNA-drug resistance associations is critical for drug screening and precision medicine. However, conventional experimental approaches remain time-consuming and labor-intensive, while existing computational methods often face challenge in capturing higher-order semantic inference from sparse prior bipartite association network. To address this, we propose MPHGNN, a heterogeneous graph convolutional network (GCN) architecture for predicting miRNA-drug resistance associations. MPHGNN constructs a miRNA-gene-drug heterogeneous network with multimodal biological features, including miRNA expression profiles, drug structural descriptors, and gene functional similarities, and leverages dual learning modules at both metapath and global levels to capture localized patterns and global representations simultaneously. Experimental results demonstrate that MPHGNN outperforms state-of-the-art methods and enhances the discriminative ability of association representations. Interpretability analyses further reveal that metapaths effectively capture underlying biological mechanisms, while the constructed heterogeneous biological network makes important contributions to prediction.

sec.p: Keywords: miRNA-drug association resistance identification, metapath, heterogeneous graph neural network, interpretability analysis
Received 2025 Sep 12; Revised 2025 Dec 17; Accepted 2026 Jan 5; Collection date 2026 Jan.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Cancer has become the first reason for death in the world with the increase of its morbidity and mortal [1]. Advances in cancer treatment have significantly improved patient survival rates and quality of life. However, patients receiving pharmacological treatment frequently develop clinically significant drug resistance, substantially diminishing therapeutic efficacy and potentially triggering tumor recurrence and metastasis, culminating in treatment failure [2]. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a class of small non-coding RNA molecules that play pivotal roles in regulating gene expression [3]. Recent studies have clarified the critical roles of miRNAs in cancer pathogenesis, and demonstrated the potential of miRNAs as therapeutic targets and regulators of drug resistance [4]. For example, recent evidence indicates that miRNA-93 modulates gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer cells through regulation of the PTEN/PI3K/Akt signaling axis [5]. Accurately predicting miRNA-drug resistance association is critical, as it not only optimizes the design of miRNA-targeted therapies but also provides key guidance for both basic and clinical research [6]. However, conventional wet-lab approaches for investigating the association are time-consuming and labour-intensive. Thus, developing computational approaches to accurately and effectively predict miRNA-drug resistance associations has become an urgent need in current research.

In recent years, deep learning and graph neural network based methods have emerged as prominent tools for molecular association prediction, such as predictions for noncoding RNA-disease associations [7–9], drug-disease associations [10, 11] and noncoding RNA-drug associations [12–14]. The existing methods can be primarily categorized into three groups: Graph learning-based methods, Deep learning-based methods and Graph contrastive framework-based methods. (i) Graph-learning-based methods explicitly model biological systems as graphs, enabling the direct capture of complex topological structures, neighborhood relationships, and dependency pathways among biological entities. Their effectiveness, nevertheless, may be influenced by the accuracy and completeness of the initially constructed biological network. Graph learning-based methods include: SubKNet, which leverages subgraph extraction and diversity-regularized graph filters for node-pair representation learning [15]; GAM-MDR, which integrates a Graph Autoencoder (GAE) with random path masking techniques to predict potential miRNA-drug resistance association [16]; GraphCDD, which integrates multimodal graph neural networks with heterogeneous data to learn node representations for predictive modelling [17]; and HBNMM, which combines graph attention networks (GATs) with multi-task learning to predict multiple bio-entity association [18]. (ii) Deep learning-based approaches are capable of automatically learning hierarchical feature representations from complex data. In bio-entity association prediction, however, the limited availability of known positive associations may pose challenges for model generalization and increase the risk of overfitting. DLST-MDA, which employs attribute information of miRNAs and drugs for prediction, diverging from conventional dependency on interaction graph data [19]; and DeepLDA, which integrates deep neural networks with graph attention to learn lncRNA-drug representations for predicting resistance associations [20]. (iii) Graph contrastive learning frameworks learn graph structural representations by maximizing the consistency between different augmented views of the same node or subgraph. Their representation performance is highly sensitive to both the contrastive strategies employed and the quality of the graphs. NDSGCL, which employs graph convolutional network (GCN) on ncRNA-drug bipartite graphs to learn feature representations by integrating local and global neighbors through contrastive learning [21]; and AGCLNDA, which employs Light Graph Convolutional Network (LightGCN) to learn vector representations, and incorporates learnable augmented and denoised view generators to address data sparsity and noise issues [22].

Despite these achievements, they have several limitations: (i) Existing methods incorporate complex information from sparse bipartite biological networks, yet fail to integrate intrinsic entity features such as expression profiles of noncoding RNAs and structural features of drugs. Entity features provide biological prior knowledge which compensates for the limitations of sparse topological structure information [23, 24]. (ii) Existing graph learning-based methods overlook the critical role of metapaths in biological network link prediction. Metapaths capture higher-order relational patterns by aggregating multi-hop connections, and discover biologically significant indirect association [25–27]. Overall, prevailing computational models exhibit fundamental limitations in integrate intrinsic biomolecular attributes and higher-order semantic patterns, consequently constraining their capacity to uncover biological associations.

To overcome these limitations, we propose MPHGNN, a heterogeneous GCN architecture for predicting miRNA-drug resistance associations. MPHGNN constructs a heterogeneous biological network to integrate miRNA-gene-drug interactions and multimodal features, including miRNA expression profiles, drug structural descriptors, and gene functional similarities. It consists of two core modules that capture higher-order biological associations at the metapath level and global network patterns. By combining metapath-driven information with global network inferences, MPHGNN can effectively capture both local biological mechanisms and system-level perspectives. Experimental results demonstrate that MPHGNN significantly improves prediction accuracy. Interpretability analyses further reveal that metapaths capture key biological mechanisms underlying potential miRNA-drug resistance associations, while node and edge importance highlights the contributions of different entities and their interactions to the predictions. Our method provides a promising strategy to identify candidate miRNAs from a large set of biomolecules, thereby supporting the study of drug resistance mechanisms, facilitating the identification of novel resistance biomarkers to guide drug selection, and revealing potential therapeutic targets to overcome resistance.

sec.title: Datasets
sec.p: To construct heterogenous network, various bio-entity associations were derived from four public sources: (i) miRNA-drug resistance associations from ncRNADrug [28], (ii) drug-gene interactions from DrugBank [29], (iii) miRNA-gene regulations from ENCORI [30], and (iv) gene–gene functional linkages from HumanNet [31] In addition, miRNA expression and drug structure information were collected from CCLE [32] and PubChem [33] respectively. Only experimentally validated miRNA-drug associations retrieved from ncRNADrug were retained. To ensure data quality and the completeness of bio-entity attribute information, we excluded miRNAs without corresponding expression profiles, drugs lacking SMILES strings, as well as redundant or ambiguous associations. The resulting network encompasses 7540 experimentally validated miRNA-drug associations, 579 drug-gene associations, 827 miRNA-gene regulatory interactions, and 5069 functional gene–gene linkages. This integrated dataset is formally denoted as .

sec.title: Method overview
sec.p: The framework of MPHGNN, as shown in Figure 1, has five main components: heterogeneous network construction, metapath generator, node aggregator, metapath embedding projector, and graph autoencoder.

caption.p: Overall framework of MPHGNN. (a) Heterogeneous network construction. The heterogeneous network is constructed with miRNA expression patterns, drug structural descriptors, and gene similarity, and the miRNA-drug-gene association network. (b) Main modules of MPHGNN: Metapath generator constructs path <miRNA ⇔ gene ⇔ gene ⇔ drug> by using validated miRNA-drug resistance associations and heterogeneous network. Node aggregator aggregates node embeddings within the metapath structure to construct representations of meta path instance. Metapath embedding projector uses an attention mechanism to obtain and update the representations of metapath. Graph autoencoder utilizes GNN encoder and MLP decoder to reconstruct the miRNA-drug resistance associations. Finally, the metapath-level-predictor and global-level-predictor relevance scores are aggregated to predict miRNA-drug resistance associations.

graphic.alt-text: Alt text: Schematic diagram of the MPHGNN framework. The figure contains two panels: (a) a heterogeneous network integrating miRNA expression data, drug structural features, gene similarity, and miRNA–drug–gene associations; and (b) a model architecture illustrating metapath generation, node aggregation along miRNA–gene–gene–drug paths, attention-based metapath embedding projection, a graph autoencoder with GNN encoder and MLP decoder, and prediction modules that combine metapath-level and global-level scores to infer miRNA–drug resistance associations.

sec.title: Performance evaluation
sec.p: To comprehensively assess the predictive performance of MPHGNN, we employed multiple widely used evaluation metrics, including the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), the area under the precision–recall curve (AUPR), Accuracy (ACC), F1-score (F1), Precision, Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) and Brier score (BS). AUC evaluates the capability of the classifier to distinguish between positive and negative samples. A higher AUC indicates stronger discriminative ability. AUPR emphasizes the balance between precision and recall, reflecting the ability to identify true positive associations. Accuracy measures the proportion of correctly predicted samples among all samples. Precision quantifies the proportion of correctly predicted positive samples among all predicted positive samples. The Brier score measures the agreement between predicted probabilities and true outcomes, providing a balanced assessment of model reliability. BS is defined as:

sec.p: In our training epoch analysis, the number of epochs varied from 10 to 50, and experiment result is illustrated in Figure 2a. From Figure 2a, we can observe that the predictive performance of MPHGNN increases first then decreases with the increasing of training epochs. As shown in Figure 2b, the performance differential across varying number of layers remained within a tight margin of ±0.2%. So, MPHGNN performs robustness to variations of layer. For different learning rate, Figure 2c demonstrates that a large learning rate may induce oscillatory divergence. Figure 2d shows that increasing the batch size from 64 to 256 yields consistent improvements in predictive performance. The larger batches may provide more stable gradient estimates. Finally, we obtained the optimal parameter combination of MPHGNN on the benchmark dataset through grid search, where the training epoch the learning rate, the batch size and the number of GNN layers are 30, 0.0001, 256, and 3, respectively.

sec.title: Comparison with other methods
sec.p: To evaluate the performance of MPHGNN in predicting miRNA-drug resistance associations, we compared it with five competitive methods: GAM-MDR [16], DeepLDA [20], AGCLDNA [22], NDSGCL [21] and SubKNet [15].

GAM-MDR integrates drug molecular structures and miRNA sequences data to predict their associations. It employs a Bernoulli distribution to select initial nodes and using random walks to mask partial paths. A GAE (GNN encoder and MLP decoder) reconstructs the network to learn node embeddings, which are then used to score and predict miRNA-drug resistance associations.

DeepLDA constructs a similarity network integrating lncRNAs and drugs. It applies GCN to extract features from the lncRNA-drug network, then refines them through GAT to obtain attention-weighted node embeddings, which are ultimately used for association prediction.

AGCLDNA utilizes LightGCN to extract neighborhood information from the ncRNA-drug bipartite graph. It leverages two learnable view generators, enhancement view generator and denoising view generator jointly create augmented graph perspectives. Through contrastive learning, self-supervised signals are generated to refine the embeddings, and association scores computed as ncRNA-drug embedding inner products.

NDSGCL leverages graph contrastive learning to predict ncRNA-drug association. The method integrates dual perspectives by constructing local structural neighbourhoods and global semantic neighbourhoods. This dual-view optimizes local and global representations through contrastive learning, preserving their distinctive features while generating refined embeddings for accurate association prediction.

SubKNet characterizes node roles across varying connection types while harnessing subgraph information sharing. The method leverages subgraph-aware representation learning to capture distinct structural features and graph-based representation to integrate global network topology. The final predictions combine these subgraph-aware and graph-level embeddings.

All the methods are trained on the benchmark dataset and evaluated on the independent test set . Table 1 and Figure 3 show the experiment results. MPHGNN attains the highest scores across most of the evaluation metrics, and its AUC and AUPR values are 0.978 and 0.937, respectively. Compared to the suboptimal method, MPHGNN improves the ACC, F1, BS and MCC by 4.30%, 8.02%, 3.94% and 10.03%, respectively. Notably, MPHGNN achieves the lowest BS among all compared methods, indicating that it not only surpasses other models in classification performance but also provides more accurate and reliable probabilistic predictions. GAM-MDR also utilizes graph autoencoders, however, it primarily relies on random path masking and lacks explicit biological guidance for feature extraction. In contrast, MPHGNN incorporates biologically meaningful metapaths to capture higher-order functional associations and potential biological mechanisms underlying drug resistance. Compared with contrastive learning frameworks such as AGCLNDA and NDSGCL, which focus on generating augmented views and integrating local–global neighbors, MPHGNN emphasizes the integration of domain knowledge through metapaths, which reduces dependence on purely data-driven augmentation strategies. However, DeepLDA relies on topological similarities in homogeneous networks and SubKNet extracts features from local subgraphs and global topology. Metapath-based method incorporates explicit biological prior knowledge, MPHGNN can capture semantically meaningful pathways beyond mere structural patterns and achieve more accurate and generalizable predictions in miRNA-drug resistance association.

sec.p: Existing miRNA-drug databases are inherently incomplete, meaning that many true associations may remain unreported. In typical supervised learning settings, these unreported pairs are usually treated as negative samples, which can potentially lead to an overestimation of model performance. To evaluate the impact of this issue on model performance, we conducted a label noise robustness experiment. Specifically, we randomly converted a small proportion of unreported pairs into positive samples to simulate the presence of false negatives in real-world data. The proportion of pseudo-positive samples was set to 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, and 0.25 relative to the number of true positive samples. The experimental results are presented in Supplementary Table S1.

It can be observed that when the noise level is low (Rate ≤ 0.1), the overall performance of all models remains relatively stable. However, as the noise ratio increases, most performance metrics of several models show a clear decline. For example, the AUC, ACC, and MCC of NDSGCL and AGCLNDA decrease significantly as the noise level increases, indicating that these models are more sensitive to synthetic negative samples. In contrast, GAM-MDR, DeepLDA, and SubKNet show smaller performance degradation, demonstrating a certain degree of noise robustness. However, as the noise level continues to increase, both GAM-MDR and SubKNet show a progressive downward trend across multiple evaluation metrics. Notably, MPHGNN consistently achieves better performance under all Rate settings, with its evaluation metrics remaining nearly unaffected by changes in noise proportion. This finding indicates that MPHGNN possesses strong robustness and generalization capability when handling noisy labels or potential false samples.

sec.title: Ablation studies
sec.p: The ablation studies were performed for exploring the contribution of each module in MPHGNN to miRNA-drug resistance association prediction. MPHGNN comprised six core modules, we compared MPHGNN with six baseline variant models, including those with attention mechanism removed (w/o Att), drug/miRNA/gene feature replaced by Xavier initialization (w/o Drug/Mi/Gene), graph autoencoder excluded (w/o GAE), and meta-module eliminated (w/o Meta). The experimental results are shown in Figure 4, from which we can observe that the performance degradation across all metrics when individual module is removed, which confirms the indispensable role of each component in miRNA-drug resistance association prediction. The performance degradation of w/o Drug, w/o Mi, and w/o Gene confirms that drug structural fingerprints, miRNA expression profiles, and gene functional similarity collectively enable accurate association prediction by uncovering latent pharmacophore-mRNA binding compatibility, post-transcription regulation specificity and pathway-mediated interaction contexts. The inferior performance of w/o GAE and w/o Meta demonstrates the indispensable yet distinct roles of global-level graph learning for capturing network topological consistency and metapath-level learning for modeling multi-hop relationship patterns. The results of w/o Att demonstrate the attention mechanism enhances the capability to prioritize critical information through learned attention weights. The experimental results demonstrate that ablating any one core module leads to significant performance degradation.

sec.title: Feature analysis
sec.p: MPHGNN representation learning capacity is investigated by examining the separability of positive and negative samples across hierarchical representation spaces, so as to verify whether MPHGNN can convert initially unstructured biological features into discriminative embeddings. We employed t-SNE to visualize the embeddings of positive and negative sample pairs in a 3D projection space. As shown in Figure 5, MPHGNN effectively separates positive and negative sample pairs into distinct clusters. In contrast, raw features and gene-associated features exhibit continuous and overlapping distributions. This result demonstrates that our proposed metapath-level and global-level learning framework significantly enhances discriminative capability between positive and negative samples.

sec.title: Interpretable exploration of MPHGNN
sec.p: To systematically investigate the interpretability of MPHGNN, we selected the highest-ranked miRNA-drug pair <miR1290, Sevoflurane> from Table 2 in Section 3.6 and visualized one representative metapath instance, as shown in Figure 6a. The representative metapath instance was selected from the highest-ranked metapaths for this target miRNA-drug pair. The top 20 ranked metapaths for each of the top 30 miRNA-drug pairs reported in Table 2 are provided in Supplementary Table S2. The score of each metapath is generated by the metapath-level predictor module of the MPHGNN. The miR1290 was upregulated and inhibited autophagy in melanoma. BECN1 is the direct functional effector of miR1290. Furthermore, POL promoted BECN1 expression though inhibition of miR1290, thus inducing melanoma-cell autophagy [36]. GSK3B phosphorylates MCL1 to trigger axonal autophagy and degeneration; phosphorylated MCL1 is ubiquitinated by FBXW7 and degraded via the proteasome, thereby releasing BECLIN1 to initiate axonal autophagy [37]. The data indicate that sevoflurane causes Tau phosphorylation, activates GSK3B, elevates IL-6, reduces PSD-95 in the hippocampus, and leads to cognitive deficits in young mice [38]. In short, this metapath paradigm demonstrates how higher-order biological relationships can systematically explain drug response mechanisms.

sec.p: The heterogeneous graph network, as a powerful paradigm for prediction, can model the multi-typed biological entities and their complex interaction. To show the roles of key biological entities and dominant information pathways, we performed an interpretability analysis by introducing HeteroGNNExplainer [39] on the constructed heterogeneous network. As shown in Figure 6b, the node importance of miRNA dominates 49.1%, followed by drug and gene entities, which account for 40.3% and 10.5% respectively. At the edge level, miRNA-drug resistance associations represent 60.7% of relational importance, which significantly surpasses miRNA-gene and gene-drug connections. The predominant contribution of miRNA node aligns with their established roles as post-transcriptional regulators. Analysis of edge-type importance in the heterogeneous graph reveals that miRNA-drug edges have the largest contribution in the prediction task, underscoring their relevance to drug response mechanisms. At the same time, miRNA-gene and gene-drug edges also contribute meaningfully, reflecting the influence of indirect regulatory pathways. Therefore, metapath-level and heterogeneous biological networks may reveal mechanisms underlying miRNA-drug resistance associations.

sec.title: Case study
sec.p: To further validate the predictive accuracy of MPHGNN, the top 30 predicted miRNA-drug resistance associations are listed in Table 2, indicating that the majority of them are supported by experimental literature. For simplicity, only one representative reference is provided for each finding. For instance, the association between hsa-mir-1290 and sevoflurane exhibits a resistant phenotype. Sevoflurane exerts its anti-glioma effects through upregulation of circRELN, which modulates glioma progression via the miR-1290/RORA signaling axis [38]. Upregulation of miR-34a downregulates MARCKS protein levels, consequently reversing lenalidomide resistance in myeloma cells [40]. MicroRNA-143 augments chemosensitivity of quercetin in gastric cancer cells by suppressing autophagy through direct targeting of GABARAPL1 [41]. Moreover, in our heterogeneous network, this miRNA-drug pair is also connected through a biologically meaningful meta-path (hsa-mir-143-3p ⇔ AP2B1 ⇔ ACTB ⇔ Quercetin), indicating that miR-143 and Quercetin may interact via shared downstream regulatory pathways. Notably, two predicted miRNA and drug pairs lack experimental support and may indicate potential biologically relevant associations. In summary, MPHGNN can predict novel miRNA-drug resistance associations and provide experimentally testable miRNA candidates to study mechanism of drug therapy.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The identification of miRNA-drug resistance associations holds significant importance in elucidating both pharmacological mechanisms and miRNA-mediated drug response. In this study, we introduce a novel computational framework designated as MPHGNN to predict miRNA-drug resistance associations. By integrating metapath generator, node aggregator, metapath embedding projector with attention mechanism and graph autoencoder, MPHGNN can effectively capture the higher-order semantic relationships. Experiment results show MPHGNN outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. Ablation validates the individual contributions of each core component. And the interpretability explorations uncover potential biological mechanisms underlying the predictions. Additionally, case studies show MPHGNN can effectively identify biologically relevant miRNA-drug resistance associations in real-world scenarios.

Although MPHGNN demonstrates promising results, further improvements are warranted: (i) MPHGNN relies on aggregated databases rather than context-specific or stratified data. Given the pronounced heterogeneity of tumors, its predictions are inherently probabilistic, making them well-suited for preliminary candidate screening, but not for context-specific or tumor-type-specific interpretation. Future work could incorporate tumor-type-specific data or stratify by clinical context, enabling more precise, context-aware predictions; (ii) drug resistance was treated as a binary outcome because most existing ncRNA-drug databases record resistance information in categorical form. However, drug resistance is inherently a continuous process, reflecting gradual changes in cellular tolerance to drugs. This binary simplification may overlook intermediate or dose-dependent resistance states, thereby providing only limited guidance for understanding drug response. Incorporating continuous drug response and multi-dose transcriptomic data could better capture the gradual, dose-dependent nature of resistance.

list-item.p: Aberrant expression of microRNAs (miRNAs) is closely linked to disease pathogenesis and therapeutic response. We propose MPHGNN, a heterogeneous graph convolutional network (GCN) for predicting miRNA-drug resistance associations.

MPHGNN integrates multimodal biological features within a miRNA-gene-drug heterogeneous network, and leverages dual metapath and global learning modules to capture both local patterns and global representations.

MPHGNN outperforms existing methods across multiple evaluation settings, and improves the discriminative power of association representations. Interpretability analyses further confirm that the heterogeneous network enhances predictive performance, while metapaths reveal underlying biological mechanisms.
